Constant-Factor Local Approximation
for Bipartite Densest Subgraph

Michael Kapralov Affiliation: EPFL    Jakub Łącki Affiliation: Google    Silvio Lattanzi Affiliation: Google    Guy Weissenberg Affiliation: EPFL
Abstract

Given a vertex vv in a large bipartite graph GG, can one quickly find a small densely connected region near vv? This is the algorithmic core of many fraud detection, community detection, and recommender systems. One would like a local algorithm, i.e., an algorithm that probes GG in only a small number of locations to find such a region. Our main contribution is the first constant-factor local approximation, independent of the maximum degree of the graph, for the classical notion of bipartite density: if the sides of a bipartite subgraph are SS and TT, its density is d⁡(S,T)≔e⁡(S,T)/|S|​|T|d(S,T)\coloneq e(S,T)/\sqrt{|S||T|}, where e⁡(S,T)e(S,T) is the number of edges between SS and TT. We consider cohesive dense subgraphs, since every dense subgraph contains a cohesive core of at least the same density. For such a cohesive dense subgraph S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T with at most kk vertices per side, our algorithm, starting from any vertex in S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T, uses Oϵ​(k4+ϵ)O_{\epsilon}(k^{4+\epsilon}) neighbor queries to find a subgraph X∪˙YX\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}Y of density Ωϵ​(d​(S,T))\Omega_{\epsilon}(d(S,T)) on Oϵ​(k2+ϵ)O_{\epsilon}(k^{2+\epsilon}) vertices, for every fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0. We improve upon the result of Andersen (2010), whose approximation guarantee depends logarithmically on the maximum degree. We complement our positive result with information-theoretic and computational limitations: the quadratic dependence on kk in the output size is essentially unavoidable for constant-factor approximation. Our main technical innovation is an adaptation of the Lovász–Simonovits curve to the bipartite density problem, based on weak-ℓp\ell_{p} norm bounds.

1 Introduction

Identifying dense bipartite subgraphs is a fundamental primitive across machine learning, network science, and web data mining. Bipartite graphs model interactions between two kinds of entities: accounts and products in e-commerce, users and multimedia content on social platforms, authors and venues in bibliometrics, or queries and destination URLs in web search (Dhillon, 2001). In fraud detection and cybersecurity, researchers search for dense bipartite subgraphs to detect botnets, astroturfing campaigns, and lockstep review manipulation, where malicious actors coordinate attacks against targeted subsets of resources (Beutel et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2016; Hooi et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2018). In web mining, dense subgraphs correspond to link-spam farms (Gibson et al., 2005) and authoritative topic hubs (Kleinberg, 1999). In computational biology, dense subgraphs are used to identify regulatory motifs in genomic DNA (Fratkin et al., 2006), analyze drug–target interaction graphs, and uncover multi-functional complexes in gene annotation networks (Saha et al., 2010).

To quantify how tightly two sets of vertices are connected, we use the bipartite density objective (Kannan and Vinay, 1999; Andersen, 2010). Throughout, G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a finite simple undirected bipartite graph with a fixed bipartition V=L∪˙RV=L\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}R and maximum degree Δ\Delta. For nonempty vertex sets S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R with e⁡(S,T)e(S,T) edges between them, their density is

d⁡(S,T)≔e⁡(S,T)|S|​|T|=e⁡(S,T)|S|⋅e⁡(S,T)|T|,d(S,T)\coloneq\frac{e(S,T)}{\sqrt{|S||T|}}=\sqrt{\frac{e(S,T)}{|S|}\cdot\frac{e(S,T)}{|T|}},

the geometric mean of the average degree from SS into TT and the average degree from TT into SS.

The maximum of d⁡(S,T)d(S,T) over all nonempty sets S,TS,T on opposite sides can be computed in polynomial time by linear programming (Charikar, 2000). However, on modern web-scale networks—frequently spanning hundreds of millions of vertices and billions of edges (Qin et al., 2015)—such global algorithms are computationally prohibitive, as their running time and memory footprint scale with the size of the entire graph. We therefore study the local formulation (Andersen, 2010): given a starting vertex vv and a target size parameter kk, find a dense bipartite subgraph in the vicinity of vv using a number of queries and running time that depend solely on kk, completely independent of the graph size |V||V| and maximum degree Δ\Delta.

Classical local clustering algorithms for low-conductance sets (Spielman and Teng, 2013; Andersen et al., 2006; Allen-Zhu et al., 2013) seek sets with few boundary edges relative to their total degree. In contrast, d⁡(S,T)d(S,T) is independent of edges leaving S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T. Dense bipartite subgraphs in interaction graphs often have many edges to the rest of the graph—for example, when fraudulent accounts add large numbers of legitimate interactions as “camouflage” (Hooi et al., 2017). With these camouflage edges, the cut conductance of S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T can approach 11. Standard random-walk and diffusion methods can then quickly leave the target, so we need local algorithms designed specifically for the bipartite density objective (Figure 1).

More formally, the local algorithm receives a starting vertex vv, an integer k≥1k\geq 1, and adjacency-list access to GG, as in Andersen (2010). We count neighbor queries: we read a specified entry of an adjacency list, or receive ⊥\bot past its end. The guarantee is measured against unknown cohesive sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R (Definition 1.1) with at most kk vertices on each side. We require the algorithm to succeed from every starting vertex in S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T, using a number of queries independent of |V||V|. An approximation ratio α≥1\alpha\geq 1 means returning nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L, Y⊆RY\subseteq R with d⁡(X,Y)≥d⁡(S,T)/αd(X,Y)\geq d(S,T)/\alpha. For a single vertex, we write e⁡(u,T)≔e⁡({u},T)e(u,T)\coloneq e(\{u\},T) and e⁡(S,w)≔e⁡(S,{w})e(S,w)\coloneq e(S,\{w\}).

We ask for approximation, not recovery: the union of the returned sets need not contain the starting vertex or intersect S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T (after adding vv to the returned set on its side, the density is at least d⁡(X,Y)/2d(X,Y)/\sqrt{2}; see Lemma B.3). A star with at least d​(S,T)2d(S,T)^{2} leaves has density at least d⁡(S,T)d(S,T) and is therefore an acceptable output.

Andersen’s algorithm can be implemented using O⁡(Δ​k2)O(\Delta k^{2}) neighbor queries and returns sets X,YX,Y with O⁡(Δ​k2)O(\Delta k^{2}) vertices each (this follows from Andersen’s analysis (Andersen, 2010, proof of Theorem 2); see also Section C.2). Its approximation ratio is bounded by O⁡(1+log2⁡(Δ/d⁡(S,T)))O(1+\log_{2}(\Delta/d(S,T))) (Andersen, 2010, Theorem 1). This bound is constant only when d⁡(S,T)=Ω⁡(Δ)d(S,T)=\Omega(\Delta). For the complete bipartite subgraph of Figure 1 with DD camouflage edges per vertex, the lower bound on the returned density is Ω⁡(k/(1+log2⁡((k+D)/k)))\Omega(k/(1+\log_{2}((k+D)/k))), which decreases as DD grows even though d⁡(S,T)=kd(S,T)=k. The density is invariant under the addition of edges outside the subgraph induced by S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T, and the guarantee is not. Whether this dependence on the maximum degree is necessary for local approximation was open.

1.1 Our results

Our main result is a constant-factor local approximation algorithm for the bipartite densest subgraph problem. We cannot guarantee success from every vertex of S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T for arbitrary target sets S,TS,T, since a vertex in S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T may have few or no edges into the opposite target set. We therefore require every target vertex to have at least half the average degree of its side within the target subgraph.

Definition 1.1 (Cohesive sets).

Nonempty sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R with e⁡(S,T)>0e(S,T)>0 are cohesive if e⁡(u,T)≥e⁡(S,T)2​|S|e(u,T)\geq\frac{e(S,T)}{2|S|} for all u∈Su\in S, and e⁡(S,w)≥e⁡(S,T)2​|T|e(S,w)\geq\frac{e(S,T)}{2|T|} for all w∈Tw\in T.

We use the term cohesiveness to formalize the minimum-degree structure already implicit in Andersen’s proof of his main theorem (Andersen, 2010, Theorem 1). For any sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R with e⁡(S,T)>0e(S,T)>0, there are cohesive subsets S∗⊆SS^{*}\subseteq S, T∗⊆TT^{*}\subseteq T of at least the same density, d⁡(S∗,T∗)≥d⁡(S,T)d(S^{*},T^{*})\geq d(S,T) (Lemma A.1). For arbitrary S,TS,T, our setting is exactly that of Andersen, whose algorithm succeeds from every vertex of subsets that are selected by a minimum-degree argument and contain at least half of the edges (see the discussion in Corollary A.2).

Theorem 1.2 (Main result).

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, all cohesive sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R with |S|,|T|≤k|S|,|T|\leq k, and every starting vertex v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T, the deterministic algorithm 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾2+ϵ​(G,v,k)\mathsf{LocalDense}_{2+\epsilon}(G,v,k) (Algorithm 2) returns nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L, Y⊆RY\subseteq R with the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    Locality and complexity: The output (X,Y)(X,Y) has Oϵ​(k2+ϵ)O_{\epsilon}(k^{2+\epsilon}) vertices, and the algorithm makes Oϵ​(k2+ϵ​min⁡{Δ​log22⁡(2​k),k2})O_{\epsilon}(k^{2+\epsilon}\min\{\Delta\log_{2}^{2}(2k),k^{2}\}) neighbor queries and runs in time O~ϵ​(k2+ϵ​min⁡{Δ,k2})\widetilde{O}_{\epsilon}(k^{2+\epsilon}\min\{\Delta,k^{2}\}).

  2. (ii)

    Constant-factor approximation: d⁡(X,Y)≥316​e​ϵ1+ϵ​d​(S,T)d(X,Y)\geq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{16\sqrt{\mathrm{e}}}\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}\,d(S,T), independent of edges outside the subgraph induced by S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T.

We complement our positive results by proving limitations on the output size:

Theorem 1.3 (Limitations on the output size, informal).

No possibly randomized algorithm with neighbor-query access that, for all cohesive sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R with kk vertices on each side, returns nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L, Y⊆RY\subseteq R with d⁡(X,Y)=Ω⁡(d⁡(S,T))d(X,Y)=\Omega(d(S,T)) with probability at least 2/32/3 from at least one vertex in S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T can guarantee an output bound of o⁡(k2)o(k^{2}) vertices on each side if either:

  1. (i)

    Unconditional: Its number of queries depends only on kk; or

  2. (ii)

    Computational: Assuming the Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis (SPCH), its running time is at most f⁡(k)​|V|cf(k)\,|V|^{c} for a constant cc and a computable function ff of kk alone.

Up to the factor kϵk^{\epsilon}, our output size is therefore the best possible in both settings. We discuss the main result in Section 2 and the limitations in Section 3.

1.2 Our technique

From power iteration to prefix sweeps.

Our starting point is Andersen’s pruned power iteration (Andersen, 2010). We maintain a nonnegative vector xx indexed by vertices and multiply it by the adjacency matrix, setting y⁡(w)≔∑ux⁡(u)y(w)\coloneq\sum_{u}x(u), where the sum is over the neighbors of ww. For now, we set aside rescaling and pruning. The mass of xx on a set QQ is ∑u∈Qx⁡(u)\sum_{u\in Q}x(u). Suppose every vertex of SS has at least aa neighbors in TT and every vertex of TT at least bb in SS. After one multiplication, the mass of yy on TT is at least aa times the mass of xx on SS, and after two, the mass on SS is at least a​bab times its original value. These bounds hold even with edges leaving the target, since all coordinates are nonnegative. By cohesiveness, there exist powers of two a,b∈[1,k]a,b\in[1,k], with a​b>d⁡(S,T)/4\sqrt{ab}>d(S,T)/4 (see Section 2.2; we remove this choice later). We cannot locate a dense pair from the growth of target mass alone: the target is unknown, and mass outside it may grow faster. Andersen extracts a dense pair from growth of the Euclidean norm. Instead we sort consecutive vectors and consider their initial segments, or prefixes. We seek a Lovász–Simonovits-type win–win (Spielman and Teng, 2013; Andersen et al., 2006): either we find a dense prefix pair in a sweep, or we obtain upper bounds on prefix sums that eventually become incompatible with the mass that remains on the target. Here set size means number of vertices, rather than volume.

The choice of norm.

Which bound on prefix sums should we use for this alternative? Write Pi​(x)P_{i}(x) for the vertices with the ii largest positive coordinates, breaking ties by identifier, and Ix​(m)≔max⁡∑u∈Q|Q|≤m⁡x⁡(u)I_{x}(m)\coloneq\max_{|Q|\leq m}\sum_{u\in Q}x(u). A natural choice is the Euclidean norm, since Ix​(m)≤‖x‖2​mI_{x}(m)\leq\|x\|_{2}\sqrt{m}. However, with only this inequality we incur a logarithmic loss when summing comparable bounds over dyadic ranges of prefix sizes (see Section 2.1). Changing the sweep alone is therefore not enough. We instead fix p>2p>2 and use the weak-ℓp\ell_{p} norm (Bennett and Sharpley, 1988, Chapter 4)

‖x‖p,∞≔supm∈{1,2,…}Ix​(m)m1−1/p.\|x\|_{p,\infty}\coloneq\sup_{m\in\{1,2,\ldots\}}\frac{I_{x}(m)}{m^{1-1/p}}\thinspace.

The bounds over dyadic ranges now form a geometric series, so we incur only a pp-dependent factor when summing them (a detailed explanation of this comparison can be found in Section C.3). More precisely, let y=x​Ay=xA, where x≥0x\geq 0 is supported on LL and AA is an L×RL\times R adjacency matrix with column sums at most B∞B_{\infty}. Let σ>0\sigma>0 be the density we aim to guarantee in the returned sets. For a prefix Pm​(y)P_{m}(y), if d⁡(Pi​(x),Pm​(y))≤σd(P_{i}(x),P_{m}(y))\leq\sigma for every prefix Pi​(x)P_{i}(x), then

Iy​(m)≤Cp​σ2/p​B∞1−2/p​‖x‖p,∞​m1−1/p,Cp≔p−1p−2.I_{y}(m)\leq C_{p}\,\sigma^{2/p}B_{\infty}^{1-2/p}\|x\|_{p,\infty}m^{1-1/p},\qquad C_{p}\coloneq\frac{p-1}{p-2}\thinspace.

If the inequality fails for Pm​(y)P_{m}(y), we find dense sets by sweeping the prefixes of xx against Pm​(y)P_{m}(y). If no prefixes exceed density σ\sigma, we take the supremum over mm to bound ‖y‖p,∞\|y\|_{p,\infty} (Sections 2.1 and A.3).

Removing the degree dependence.

The logarithm is gone, but the column sums remain. For the full adjacency matrix, we only know the bound B∞=ΔB_{\infty}=\Delta on the column sums, where Δ\Delta is the maximum degree. Since a​b>d⁡(S,T)/4\sqrt{ab}>d(S,T)/4, we obtain a constant-factor approximation if we can guarantee density σ\sigma equal to a fixed fraction of a​b\sqrt{ab}, depending only on pp. The upper bound on the norm after two steps has factor Cp2​σ4/p​Δ2−4/pC_{p}^{2}\sigma^{4/p}\Delta^{2-4/p}, compared with the factor a​bab for the mass on SS. To make the norm factor smaller than a​bab, we need σ<Cp−p/2a​b(a​b/Δ)(p−2)/2\sigma<C_{p}^{-p/2}\sqrt{ab}(\sqrt{ab}/\Delta)^{(p-2)/2}, at the cost of an additional approximation factor (Δ/a​b)(p−2)/2(\Delta/\sqrt{ab})^{(p-2)/2}.

After rescaling, we want the target mass to grow while the weak norm decreases over pairs of steps. For a step from LL to RR, we use peeling to bound the number of selected edges incident to each vertex in RR while keeping enough target edges. We repeatedly remove a vertex in RR with at most b/2b/2 remaining edges and select those edges, or a vertex in the current support with at most a/4a/4 remaining edges and discard those edges. If vertices remain but neither removal is possible, their density exceeds a​b/8\sqrt{ab/8} (Section 2.2). If every vertex is removed, each vertex in RR has at most b/2b/2 selected edges, while at least 3​a/43a/4 edges into TT are selected at each vertex of S∩supp⁡(x)S\cap\operatorname{supp}(x). Let AA be the adjacency matrix of the selected edges and set y=(2/b)​x​Ay=(2/b)xA, so that the weighted column sums are at most one. For σ≔3​a​b/(4​Cpp/2)\sigma\coloneq\sqrt{3ab}/(4C_{p}^{p/2}), we either find prefixes of density greater than σ\sigma, or

∑w∈Ty⁡(w)≥3​a2​b​∑u∈Sx⁡(u),‖y‖p,∞≤(3​a4​b)1/p​‖x‖p,∞.\sum_{w\in T}y(w)\geq\frac{3a}{2b}\sum_{u\in S}x(u),\qquad\|y\|_{p,\infty}\leq\left(\frac{3a}{4b}\right)^{1/p}\|x\|_{p,\infty}\thinspace.

For the reverse step, we exchange aa and bb. If no dense sets are returned in either step, then after two steps without pruning the mass on SS is at least 9/49/4 times its earlier value, while the weak norm is at most (3/4)2/p(3/4)^{2/p} times its earlier value. Crucially, neither factor now depends on Δ\Delta (Section 2.3).

The local search.

We are now ready to combine the ideas above and present the algorithm. So far, we have assumed that suitable degree bounds a,ba,b are known. In reality, since they are unknown, we run a search for every pair of powers of two a,b∈[1,k]a,b\in[1,k] and return the densest candidate. Assume v∈Lv\in L, exchanging the sides if necessary. Each search starts with x0=1vx_{0}=\mathbbm{1}_{v}, the vector equal to one at vv and zero elsewhere, and alternates between the sides. At step tt, the algorithm reads at most ⌈σ2⌉\lceil\sigma^{2}\rceil entries of the adjacency list of each vertex in supp⁡(xt)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}). If it finds that many neighbors in one list, it returns a star of density at least σ\sigma. If no star is returned, all these adjacency lists have been read completely. The algorithm then peels the edges incident to the support of xtx_{t} and, unless dense sets are returned, performs the rescaled multiplication and sets coordinates below δ\delta to zero. We choose δ\delta to keep the support small without losing too much target mass.

We abandon the guess if the pruned vector zz is zero and otherwise set xt+1=zx_{t+1}=z only if its weak norm satisfies the bound from the inequalities above, which decreases over pairs of steps. If this bound is exceeded, we sweep xtx_{t} against the shortest prefix of zz whose sum exceeds the corresponding bound. This prefix’s vertices and sum are unchanged by pruning, so we find dense sets.

For the degree bounds chosen using cohesiveness and v∈Sv\in S, we measure target mass with a factor b/ab/a on TT and no factor on SS. Before pruning, this mass is at least 3/23/2 times its previous value, and we choose δ\delta so that the loss during pruning is at most 1/21/2. The weighted mass therefore stays at least one, its initial value, and the vector never becomes zero. At every even step reached by the search,

1≤∑u∈Sxt​(u)≤‖xt‖p,∞​k1−1/p≤(3/4)t/p​k1−1/p.1\leq\sum_{u\in S}x_{t}(u)\leq\|x_{t}\|_{p,\infty}k^{1-1/p}\leq(3/4)^{t/p}k^{1-1/p}\thinspace.

After Op​(log2⁡(2​k))O_{p}(\log_{2}(2k)) steps, the right-hand side would be less than one, so the search must return sets of density at least σ\sigma (Section 2.3).

1.3 Related Work

Spielman and Teng (2013) used the Lovász–Simonovits curve (Lovász and Simonovits, 1990; Lovász and Simonovits, 1993) to analyze their local partitioning algorithm Nibble, and Andersen et al. (2006) adapted this analysis to personalized PageRank. Other local graph-partitioning algorithms use heat-kernel PageRank (Chung, 2009) or evolving sets (Andersen et al., 2016), and local clustering by pp-norm flow diffusions and pp-norm cuts (Fountoulakis et al., 2020; Liu and Gleich, 2020) has been extended to vertex attributes and noisy labels (Yang and Fountoulakis, 2023; Back de Luca et al., 2024). Local algorithms for dense bipartite-like subgraphs (Peng, 2012; Li and Peng, 2013; Macgregor and Sun, 2021) minimize the bipartiteness ratio, a cut objective analogous to conductance.

Local and seeded variants of densest subgraph have also been studied from a practical perspective. When densest subgraphs are extracted sequentially, fragmented sub-regions of a single dominant global core may be returned while distinct local communities are missed. Qin et al. (2015) therefore introduced locally densest subgraphs (LDS), based on ρ\rho-compact subgraphs, with structural core bounds and pruning techniques for exact verification on billion-edge graphs, but their algorithm traverses the whole graph. Dai et al. (2022) introduced the anchored densest subgraph (ADS) problem, with explicit edge or vertex penalties for expanding beyond a specified reference set, and solved it via localized parametric flow networks. Huang et al. (2024) generalized this formulation to hypergraphs using negative supermodular optimization, with strongly localized routines when the penalization parameter is sufficiently large. For dense-block discovery in fraud detection, Hooi et al. (2017) gave a camouflage-resistant algorithm for the whole graph.

The local problem of Andersen (2010) was revisited by Liu (2026, Theorems 1.2.2 and 1.2.3), who obtains an output size of O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}) with Andersen’s approximation ratio, and O⁡(k1+ϵ)O(k^{1+\epsilon}) with a ratio that also depends on |V||V|. The techniques involved are different from ours and are based on spectral analysis, degree sorting, and majorization. Our algorithm, with ϵ=1/⌈log2⁡(2​k)⌉\epsilon=1/\lceil\log_{2}(2k)\rceil, also returns O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}) vertices, using O⁡(k4)O(k^{4}) neighbor queries with an O⁡(log2⁡(2​k))O(\log_{2}(2k)) approximation ratio, independent of Δ\Delta (Corollary B.4).

2 The local algorithm and its analysis

Our algorithm is based on an alternating power iteration from the starting vertex: with x0≔1vx_{0}\coloneq\mathbbm{1}_{v}, it repeatedly multiplies the current vector by the adjacency matrix of a subgraph of GG and then prunes, alternating between the two sides. For suitable degree guesses, the mass inside a cohesive target grows by a factor of at least 9/49/4 over two weighted steps, before accounting for pruning. The target is unknown to the algorithm, and the mass outside it may grow as well, so we cannot identify dense sets from growth alone. For the analysis, we compare prefixes: either prefixes P,QP,Q of consecutive vectors have density d⁡(P,Q)>σd(P,Q)>\sigma and the algorithm returns them, or the next prefix sums are bounded in terms of the current ones, with geometrically decreasing bounds over pairs of steps. This cannot last forever: the target has at most kk vertices per side, but its mass on the starting side stays at least one at every even step.

We use neighbor queries with fixed adjacency-list orders and distinct vertex identifiers. Vectors are row vectors indexed by vertices, with indicators 1S\mathbbm{1}_{S}, 1v≔1{v}\mathbbm{1}_{v}\coloneq\mathbbm{1}_{\{v\}} and support supp⁡(x)≔{u:x⁡(u)≠0}\operatorname{supp}(x)\coloneq\{u:x(u)\neq 0\}. Vectors are restricted or extended by zero to match matrix indices. For any subgraph HH of GG, numbers of edges and densities in HH are denoted by eH​(S,T)e_{H}(S,T) and dH​(S,T)d_{H}(S,T), and NG​(U)N_{G}(U) denotes the set of neighbors of U⊆VU\subseteq V in GG.

2.1 Prefix sweeps

In a step of the iteration from LL to RR, the current vector x≥0x\geq 0 is supported on LL and the next vector is y≔x​Ay\coloneq xA, where AA is the adjacency matrix of a subgraph of GG, so that each coordinate y⁡(w)y(w) is the sum of x⁡(u)x(u) over the neighbors uu of ww in this subgraph. To compare the largest coordinates of yy with those of xx, we adapt the Lovász–Simonovits curve (Lovász and Simonovits, 1990; Lovász and Simonovits, 1993) to density: in place of the curve we use Ix​(m)I_{x}(m), the largest mass of the current vector on mm vertices, and in place of a sweep set of low conductance we look for prefixes P,QP,Q with d⁡(P,Q)>σd(P,Q)>\sigma, where σ>0\sigma>0 is a density threshold, fixed in Equation 4.

Definition 2.1 (Prefix sums and the weak norm [Spielman and Teng, 2013, equation (3); Bennett and Sharpley, 1988, Chapter 4]).

For a vector x≥0x\geq 0 indexed by a finite set and ℓ≔|supp⁡(x)|\ell\coloneq|\operatorname{supp}(x)|, write x(1),…,x(ℓ)x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(\ell)} for its positive coordinates in nonincreasing order, with ties broken by identifier, and set x(i)≔0x_{(i)}\coloneq 0 for i>ℓi>\ell. where mm is a nonnegative integer and IxI_{x} is extended to real arguments s≥0s\geq 0 by linear interpolation between consecutive integers, with Ix​(0)=0I_{x}(0)=0. In particular, Ix​(s)≤‖x‖p,∞​s1−1/pI_{x}(s)\leq\|x\|_{p,\infty}s^{1-1/p} for every s>0s>0.

Definition 2.2 (Column-sum bound).

A nonnegative matrix AA has column-sum bound B∞B_{\infty} if ∑uAu​w≤B∞\sum_{u}A_{uw}\leq B_{\infty} for every column ww.

After sorting yy, we take a prefix Pm​(y)P_{m}(y), whose sum is Iy​(m)I_{y}(m), and in a sweep we look for a prefix Pi​(x)P_{i}(x) with d⁡(Pi​(x),Pm​(y))>σd(P_{i}(x),P_{m}(y))>\sigma. If there is none, then there are at most σ​i​m\sigma\sqrt{im} edges between Pi​(x)P_{i}(x) and Pm​(y)P_{m}(y) for every ii. For p>2p>2 and a column-sum bound B∞B_{\infty} for AA (Definition 2.2),

Iy​(m)≤Cp​σ2/p​B∞1−2/p​‖x‖p,∞​m1−1/p,where ​Cp≔p−1p−2.I_{y}(m)\leq C_{p}\,\sigma^{2/p}B_{\infty}^{1-2/p}\|x\|_{p,\infty}m^{1-1/p},\qquad\text{where }C_{p}\coloneq\frac{p-1}{p-2}\thinspace. (2)

This bound is a special case of Proposition A.4, proved in Section A.3 by summation by parts. In the proof, we use the smaller of two bounds for the number of edges from Pi​(x)P_{i}(x) into Pm​(y)P_{m}(y) in the subgraph represented by AA: σ​i​m\sigma\sqrt{im} from the density assumption and B∞​mB_{\infty}m from the column sums. Whenever Iy​(m)I_{y}(m) exceeds the right side of Equation 2, the algorithm finds a prefix Pi​(x)P_{i}(x) with d⁡(Pi​(x),Pm​(y))>σd(P_{i}(x),P_{m}(y))>\sigma in the sweep. If no such prefixes exist for any mm, then ‖y‖p,∞≤Cp​σ2/p​B∞1−2/p​‖x‖p,∞\|y\|_{p,\infty}\leq C_{p}\sigma^{2/p}B_{\infty}^{1-2/p}\|x\|_{p,\infty}.

The bound holds only for p>2p>2: for p=2p=2, we obtain a logarithmic factor in place of CpC_{p}, as in the guarantee of Andersen (2010), to which we compare ours in Appendix C. For the adjacency matrix of GG itself, whose column sums are the degrees, we can only take B∞≔ΔB_{\infty}\coloneq\Delta, so that the bound contains a factor Δ1−2/p\Delta^{1-2/p}, even though d⁡(S,T)d(S,T) is independent of edges outside the subgraph induced by S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T. To keep σ\sigma a fixed fraction of d⁡(S,T)d(S,T), we therefore need to bound B∞B_{\infty} independently of Δ\Delta.

2.2 Vertex peeling

For each multiplication, we select edges by peeling: we repeatedly remove a vertex of low degree, selecting its remaining edges if it is on the side of the next vector, so that its column sum is small, and discarding them if it is on the side of the current vector, so that only a few of its edges are discarded. For each target vertex in the support, most edges into the opposite target set are selected for multiplication. The thresholds for low degree are fractions of the degrees a,ba,b guaranteed by cohesiveness.

Lemma 2.3 (Degree guesses for cohesive sets).

For cohesive sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R, there are powers of two a,b≥1a,b\geq 1, depending only on S,TS,T, such that e⁡(u,T)≥ae(u,T)\geq a for every u∈Su\in S, e⁡(S,w)≥be(S,w)\geq b for every w∈Tw\in T, and a​b>d⁡(S,T)/4\sqrt{ab}>d(S,T)/4. For every kk with |S|,|T|≤k|S|,|T|\leq k, a,b≤ka,b\leq k, a​|S|≤2​b​ka|S|\leq 2bk and b​|T|≤2​a​kb|T|\leq 2ak.

The proof is in Section A.1. Since a,ba,b depend on unknown S,TS,T, the algorithm tries all pairs of powers of two in [1,k][1,k].

For a step from LL to RR with U≔supp⁡(x)U\coloneq\operatorname{supp}(x), the neighborhood graph of UU is H≔(U∪˙W,F)H\coloneq(U\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}W,F), where W≔NG​(U)W\coloneq N_{G}(U) is the set of neighbors of UU and FF is the set of edges incident to UU. (For a step from RR to LL, we argue in the same way after exchanging aa and bb.) We seek a set F′⊆FF^{\prime}\subseteq F of selected edges such that every w∈Ww\in W is incident to at most b/2b/2 selected edges and every u∈Uu\in U to at most a/4a/4 discarded edges. With each selected edge assigned weight 2/b2/b, the weighted matrix has column-sum bound B∞=1B_{\infty}=1. Each u∈S∩Uu\in S\cap U has at least aa edges into TT, of which at most a/4a/4 are discarded, so at least 3​a/43a/4 of its edges into TT belong to F′F^{\prime}, regardless of its degree in GG. Hence

∑w∈Ty⁡(w)≥3​a2​b​∑u∈Sx⁡(u).\sum_{w\in T}y(w)\geq\frac{3a}{2b}\sum_{u\in S}x(u). (3)

Here ∑u∈S∩Ux⁡(u)=∑u∈Sx⁡(u)\sum_{u\in S\cap U}x(u)=\sum_{u\in S}x(u) since U=supp⁡(x)U=\operatorname{supp}(x). 𝖯𝖾𝖾𝗅\mathsf{Peel} (Algorithm 1) selects edges by removing low-degree vertices, or returns dense subsets of the vertices it cannot remove.

If 𝖯𝖾𝖾𝗅\mathsf{Peel} removes every vertex, then an edge belongs to F′F^{\prime} exactly when its endpoint in WW is removed before its endpoint in UU (line 7). Thus every w∈Ww\in W has at most b/2b/2 selected edges and every u∈Uu\in U at most a/4a/4 discarded edges, since these are its remaining edges when it is removed (line 4). If vertices remain, then every vertex of U∗U_{*} has more than a/4a/4 neighbors in W∗W_{*} and every vertex of W∗W_{*} more than b/2b/2 neighbors in U∗U_{*} (line 4), so that dH​(U∗,W∗)>a​b/8d_{H}(U_{*},W_{*})>\sqrt{ab/8}. 2.3 The algorithm and its guarantees

𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾p\mathsf{LocalDense}_{p} (Algorithm 2) keeps the edge from vv to its first neighbor as the first candidate, so that the output is nonempty with density at least one (lines 4 to 7). By guessing a,ba,b among the powers of two in [1,k][1,k] (line 8), we lose only a constant factor in the approximation. To keep the computation local, 𝖲𝖾𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗁p\mathsf{Search}_{p} reads at most ⌈σ2⌉\lceil\sigma^{2}\rceil entries of each adjacency list and returns a star if it finds that many neighbors, since a star with that many leaves has density at least σ\sigma (line 20). It accepts the pruned vector as the next one only if it passes the weak-norm test of line 26, analyzed below.

Output size and locality.

Every positive coordinate of xtx_{t} is at least δ\delta and ‖xt‖p,∞≤Kt1/p\|x_{t}\|_{p,\infty}\leq K_{t}^{1/p}, so, by the choice of parameters in Equation 4,

|supp⁡(xt)|≤Kt​δ−p≤(4​k)p​(3/4)t,∑t|supp⁡(xt)|≤4​(4​k)p,|\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})|\leq K_{t}\delta^{-p}\leq(4k)^{p}(3/4)^{t},\qquad\sum_{t}|\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})|\leq 4(4k)^{p}, (6)

and each set returned by a sweep or by peeling has at most (4​k)p(4k)^{p} vertices (Lemma B.1(d)), so the output has Op​(kp)O_{p}(k^{p}) vertices. Every vertex of supp⁡(xt+1)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t+1}) has a neighbor in supp⁡(xt)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}), so the sets returned at step tt lie within distance t+1t+1 of vv, where t≤p​log4/3⁡(4​k)t\leq p\log_{4/3}(4k) by Equation 6. In particular, for p=2+ϵp=2+\epsilon, every returned vertex lies within distance Oϵ​(log2⁡(2​k))O_{\epsilon}(\log_{2}(2k)) of vv (Lemma B.3).

The algorithm makes Op​(kp​min⁡{(Δ+1)​log22⁡(2​k),k2})O_{p}\!\left(k^{p}\min\{(\Delta+1)\log_{2}^{2}(2k),\ k^{2}\}\right) neighbor queries (Section B.2).

Constant approximation.

We prove that, for every p>2p>2 and S,T,k,vS,T,k,v as in Theorem 1.2, the output (X,Y)(X,Y) of 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾p​(G,v,k)\mathsf{LocalDense}_{p}(G,v,k) satisfies

d(X,Y)>316Cp−p/2d(S,T).d(X,Y)>\frac{\sqrt{3}}{16}\,C_{p}^{-p/2}\,d(S,T). (7)

We choose (a,b)(a,b) as in Lemma 2.3 and suppose first that v∈Sv\in S. By the induction above, z≠0z\neq 0 at every pruning step in the search with guess (a,b)(a,b). The search cannot continue indefinitely, since 1≤∑u∈Sxt​(u)≤(3/4)t/p​k1−1/p1\leq\sum_{u\in S}x_{t}(u)\leq(3/4)^{t/p}k^{1-1/p} at every even step. Thus 𝖲𝖾𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗁p\mathsf{Search}_{p} returns sets of density at least σ\sigma within Op​(log2⁡(2​k))O_{p}(\log_{2}(2k)) steps. Since a​b>d⁡(S,T)/4\sqrt{ab}>d(S,T)/4, their density satisfies Equation 7. For v∈Tv\in T, we exchange L,RL,R and a,ba,b. All other searches also terminate by Equation 6, and 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾p\mathsf{LocalDense}_{p} returns the densest candidate. For ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and p≔2+ϵp\coloneq 2+\epsilon, we obtain the guarantees of Theorem 1.2, with approximation ratio O⁡(1+1/ϵ)O(1+1/\epsilon), by direct calculation from Equations 7 and 6, using Cp−p/2≥ϵ/(e(1+ϵ))C_{p}^{-p/2}\geq\epsilon/(\sqrt{\mathrm{e}}(1+\epsilon)); see Section B.3 for details.

3 Limitations on improving the output size

For a target with at most kk vertices per side, our algorithm returns Oϵ​(k2+ϵ)O_{\epsilon}(k^{2+\epsilon}) vertices with a constant approximation ratio. Can the output be reduced to O⁡(k)O(k) or o⁡(k2)o(k^{2}) while keeping the approximation ratio constant? The threshold k2k^{2} appears because we ask for approximation rather than recovery: a star with k2k^{2} leaves has density kk and is as dense as any target with at most kk vertices per side, whereas a star with o⁡(k2)o(k^{2}) leaves has density o⁡(k)o(k). We rule out output size ϕ⁡(k)=o⁡(k2)\phi(k)=o(k^{2}) per side in two settings:

  • •

    Restricted queries. If the worst-case number of queries is bounded by a function of kk alone, or more generally is o⁡(Δ)o(\Delta) for every fixed kk, while computation between queries is unrestricted, then, on some instance and from every target vertex, even a randomized algorithm fails with probability at least 2/32/3 to return a constant approximation. We choose kk centers per side uniformly among many disjoint stars and place the edges of a complete bipartite subgraph at uniformly chosen adjacency-list positions. We compare runs before and after this modification using the same algorithmic randomness. Unless the algorithm receives different answers or includes a target center other than the starting vertex in its output, any returned sets have density at most 2​ϕ​(k)=o⁡(k)\sqrt{2\phi(k)}=o(k), whereas the target has density kk. By summing the success probabilities over target vertices and averaging over the random construction, we obtain one graph on which the algorithm fails with probability at least 2/32/3 from every target vertex. The formal statement is Theorem D.2, proved in Section D.1.

  • •

    Restricted running time. If the algorithm may read the entire graph but must run in time f⁡(k)​|V|O⁡(1)f(k)|V|^{O(1)} for a computable function ff of kk, the limitation is that we need to find not only a dense subgraph, but also a small one. For a graph JJ promised to contain a kk-clique, the two copies S,TS,T of the clique in its bipartite double cover have d⁡(S,T)=k−1d(S,T)=k-1. From returned sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)=Ω⁡(k)d(X,Y)=\Omega(k) and |X|,|Y|≤ϕ⁡(k)|X|,|Y|\leq\phi(k), we extract a set UU of kk vertices of JJ spanning Ω⁡(k3/(k+ϕ⁡(k)))\Omega\!\left({k^{3}}/{(k+\phi(k))}\right) edges. Since the optimal kk-vertex subgraph has (k2)\binom{k}{2} edges, the approximation ratio for Densest kk-Subgraph would be O⁡(1+ϕ⁡(k)/k)=o⁡(k)O(1+\phi(k)/k)=o(k), which under the Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis (SPCH) of Manurangsi et al. (2021) is impossible in this running time, even with randomization. The formal statement is Theorem D.8, proved in Section D.2.2. Under ETH, we obtain a weaker output-size bound by the same reduction (Theorem D.12, proved in Section D.2.3).

4 Conclusion

We give the first constant-factor local approximation algorithm for the bipartite densest subgraph problem, with output size, number of queries, and running time depending on kk alone (Theorem 1.2). Like the density itself, the guarantee does not depend on edges outside the subgraph induced by S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T.

The main technical question left unanswered is the following: while sub-quadratic output is impossible in the settings of Section 3, quadratic output is not ruled out, and we leave open whether it is possible to achieve a constant-factor approximation with output of size O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}).

Beyond improving the output size and approximation ratio, is it possible, under suitable assumptions, to ensure that the returned sets overlap with the target sets? Such results are known in the case of conductance, i.e., the classical application of the Lovász–Simonovits curve—see, for example, Yang and Fountoulakis (2023); Back de Luca et al. (2024).

Appendix A Technical lemmas for the local algorithm

We prove the statements deferred from Sections 1 and 2.

A.1 Cohesive subsets and degree guesses

Lemma A.1 (Existence of cohesive subsets).

For all sets S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R with e⁡(S,T)>0e(S,T)>0, there are cohesive subsets S∗⊆SS^{*}\subseteq S and T∗⊆TT^{*}\subseteq T satisfying d⁡(S∗,T∗)≥d⁡(S,T)d(S^{*},T^{*})\geq d(S,T).

Proof.

Choose nonempty sets S∗⊆SS^{*}\subseteq S and T∗⊆TT^{*}\subseteq T maximizing d⁡(S∗,T∗)d(S^{*},T^{*}). Then d⁡(S∗,T∗)≥d⁡(S,T)>0d(S^{*},T^{*})\geq d(S,T)>0. For u∈S∗u\in S^{*}, the bound e⁡(u,T∗)≥e⁡(S∗,T∗)/(2​|S∗|)e(u,T^{*})\geq e(S^{*},T^{*})/(2|S^{*}|) is trivial if S∗={u}S^{*}=\{u\}. Otherwise, by maximality, d⁡(S∗∖{u},T∗)≤d⁡(S∗,T∗)d(S^{*}\setminus\{u\},T^{*})\leq d(S^{*},T^{*}), that is,

e⁡(S∗,T∗)−e⁡(u,T∗)(|S∗|−1)​|T∗|≤e⁡(S∗,T∗)|S∗|​|T∗|.\frac{e(S^{*},T^{*})-e(u,T^{*})}{\sqrt{(|S^{*}|-1)|T^{*}|}}\leq\frac{e(S^{*},T^{*})}{\sqrt{|S^{*}||T^{*}|}}\thinspace.

Rearranging and using 1−t≤1−t/2\sqrt{1-t}\leq 1-t/2, we get

1−e⁡(u,T∗)e⁡(S∗,T∗)≤1−1|S∗|≤1−12​|S∗|,1-\frac{e(u,T^{*})}{e(S^{*},T^{*})}\leq\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{|S^{*}|}}\leq 1-\frac{1}{2|S^{*}|}\thinspace,

so e⁡(u,T∗)≥e⁡(S∗,T∗)/(2​|S∗|)e(u,T^{*})\geq e(S^{*},T^{*})/(2|S^{*}|). By symmetry, e⁡(S∗,w)≥e⁡(S∗,T∗)/(2​|T∗|)e(S^{*},w)\geq e(S^{*},T^{*})/(2|T^{*}|) for every w∈T∗w\in T^{*}, so S∗,T∗S^{*},T^{*} are cohesive. ∎

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and all sets S⊆LS\subseteq L, T⊆RT\subseteq R with e⁡(S,T)>0e(S,T)>0 and |S|,|T|≤k|S|,|T|\leq k, there are S′⊆SS^{\prime}\subseteq S and T′⊆TT^{\prime}\subseteq T with e⁡(S′,T′)≥e⁡(S,T)/2e(S^{\prime},T^{\prime})\geq e(S,T)/2 such that, from every starting vertex v∈S′∪˙T′v\in S^{\prime}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T^{\prime}, the algorithm 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾2+ϵ​(G,v,k)\mathsf{LocalDense}_{2+\epsilon}(G,v,k) satisfies (i) of Theorem 1.2 and its output (X,Y)(X,Y) satisfies d⁡(X,Y)≥332​e​ϵ1+ϵ​d​(S,T)d(X,Y)\geq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{32\sqrt{\mathrm{e}}}\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}\,d(S,T).

Since e⁡(S,T)≤|S|​|T|e(S,T)\leq|S||T|, both a0a_{0} and b0b_{0} are at most k/4k/4. By Equation 17, d⁡(X,Y)>332​e​ϵ1+ϵ​d​(S,T)d(X,Y)>\frac{\sqrt{3}}{32\sqrt{\mathrm{e}}}\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}\,d(S,T). The bounds in (i) hold for every starting vertex by Theorem B.2. ∎

A.2 Weak-ℓp\ell_{p} preliminaries and pruning

Lemma A.3 (Prefix sums, support size, and pruning).

For a nonzero vector x≥0x\geq 0 with ℓ≔|supp⁡(x)|\ell\coloneq|\operatorname{supp}(x)|, p≥2p\geq 2 and δ>0\delta>0:

  1. (a)

    The supremum in the definition of ‖x‖p,∞\|x\|_{p,\infty} is attained at an integer m≤ℓm\leq\ell, that is,

    ‖x‖p,∞=max1≤m≤ℓ⁡Ix​(m)m1−1/p.\|x\|_{p,\infty}=\max_{1\leq m\leq\ell}\frac{I_{x}(m)}{m^{1-1/p}}\thinspace. (9)
  2. (b)

    If every positive coordinate of xx is at least δ\delta, then ℓ≤‖x‖p,∞p/δp\ell\leq\|x\|_{p,\infty}^{p}/\delta^{p}.

  3. (c)

    For y≥0y\geq 0 and z≔prune⁡(δ,y)z\coloneq\operatorname{prune}(\delta,y), z≤yz\leq y, every positive coordinate of zz is at least δ\delta, and

    0≤∑w∈Q(y⁡(w)−z⁡(w))≤δ​|Q|(Q⊆V).0\leq\sum_{w\in Q}\bigl(y(w)-z(w)\bigr)\leq\delta|Q|\qquad(Q\subseteq V)\thinspace. (10)
Proof of Lemma A.3.

We prove each item below.

  1. (a)

    On (0,1](0,1] the ratio Ix​(s)/s1−1/p=x(1)​s1/pI_{x}(s)/s^{1-1/p}=x_{(1)}s^{1/p} increases, and for s>ℓs>\ell the numerator is constant while the denominator increases. On each interval [i−1,i][i-1,i] with 2≤i≤ℓ2\leq i\leq\ell, IxI_{x} is linear (Definition 2.1) and s1−1/ps^{1-1/p} is concave. With cc the maximum of the ratio over this interval, Ix​(s)−c​s1−1/pI_{x}(s)-cs^{1-1/p} is convex with maximum zero, and a convex function attains its maximum at an endpoint of the interval, so the ratio equals cc at an endpoint. Hence the supremum is attained at an integer m≤ℓm\leq\ell.

  2. (b)

    Every positive coordinate is at least δ\delta, so ℓ​δ≤Ix​(ℓ)≤‖x‖p,∞​ℓ1−1/p\ell\delta\leq I_{x}(\ell)\leq\|x\|_{p,\infty}\ell^{1-1/p} by Definition 2.1, and hence ℓ≤‖x‖p,∞p/δp\ell\leq\|x\|_{p,\infty}^{p}/\delta^{p}.

Remark.

The norm ‖x‖p,∞\|x\|_{p,\infty} is the norm ‖x‖(p,∞)\|x\|_{(p,\infty)} of Bennett and Sharpley [1988, Chapter 4] on the weak-ℓp\ell_{p} sequence space, the Lorentz space ℓp,∞\ell_{p,\infty}. It lies between the quasinorm supii1/p​x(i)\sup_{i}i^{1/p}x_{(i)} and p/(p−1)p/(p-1) times that quasinorm.

B.2 Query complexity, running time, and locality

Graph access.

The algorithm accesses GG through neighbor queries. Each adjacency list has a fixed order. When the algorithm makes a query (u,i)(u,i) for an integer i≥1i\geq 1, it receives the iith neighbor of uu, or ⊥\bot if i>deg⁡(u)i>\deg(u), where deg⁡(u)\deg(u) is the degree of uu. To read the list to its end, the algorithm makes deg⁡(u)+1\deg(u)+1 queries. We assume that the side of a vertex can be read from its identifier. We count neighbor queries and elementary operations at unit cost, including reads, copies, and comparisons of vertex identifiers. For Θ⁡(log⁡|V|)\Theta(\log|V|)-bit identifiers, reading an identifier takes Θ⁡(log⁡|V|)\Theta(\log|V|) bit operations.

Theorem B.2 (Local computation).

For p>2p>2, k≥1k\geq 1 and every starting vertex vv, the algorithm 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾p​(G,v,k)\mathsf{LocalDense}_{p}(G,v,k) terminates. If vv is isolated, it returns ⊥\bot after one query. Otherwise, the output has at most 2​(4​k)p2(4k)^{p} vertices and density at least one, the number of neighbor queries is at most

1+4​(4​k)p​min⁡{(Δ+1)​(1+⌊log2⁡k⌋)2, 4​k2},1+4(4k)^{p}\min\left\{(\Delta+1)(1+\lfloor\log_{2}k\rfloor)^{2},\ 4k^{2}\right\}\thinspace, (15)

and the running time is

Op​(min⁡{Δ​kp​log23⁡(2​k),kp+2​log2⁡(2​k)}).O_{p}\!\left(\min\left\{\Delta k^{p}\log_{2}^{3}(2k),\ k^{p+2}\log_{2}(2k)\right\}\right)\thinspace. (16)
Proof of Theorem B.2.

If vv is isolated, the first query is answered with ⊥\bot, and 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾p\mathsf{LocalDense}_{p} returns ⊥\bot as well (line 5). Otherwise, every search terminates by Lemma B.1(c). By Lemma B.1(d), the sets returned by the searches have at most (4​k)p(4k)^{p} vertices per side, so the output has at most 2​(4​k)p2(4k)^{p} vertices. Its density is at least one because the initial edge is a candidate.

By Lemma B.1(b), for each guess (a,b)(a,b), the algorithm scans at most ∑t|supp⁡(xt)|≤4​(4​k)p\sum_{t}|\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})|\leq 4(4k)^{p} adjacency lists in total, with at most min⁡{Δ+1,⌈σ2⌉}≤min⁡{Δ+1,a​b}\min\{\Delta+1,\lceil\sigma^{2}\rceil\}\leq\min\{\Delta+1,ab\} queries per list by Lemma B.1(d). Including the initial query, the total is at most

1+4​(4​k)p​∑a,bmin⁡{Δ+1,a​b},1+4(4k)^{p}\sum_{a,b}\min\{\Delta+1,ab\}\thinspace,

where there are (1+⌊log2⁡k⌋)2(1+\lfloor\log_{2}k\rfloor)^{2} guesses and

∑a,ba​b=(∑j=0⌊log2⁡k⌋2j)2<4​k2.\sum_{a,b}ab=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\log_{2}k\rfloor}2^{j}\right)^{2}<4k^{2}\thinspace.

Thus the number of queries is at most Equation 15.

For the running time, we consider a step in which no star is returned, with the neighborhood graph H=(U∪˙W,F)H=(U\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}W,F) of U≔supp⁡(xt)U\coloneq\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}). Every vertex of UU has a neighbor, since vv has positive degree and every vertex of supp⁡(xt+1)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t+1}) is joined to supp⁡(xt)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}) by a selected edge (line 10), so |U|+|W|≤2​|F||U|+|W|\leq 2|F|. By Lemma B.1(b), |U|≤(4​k)p|U|\leq(4k)^{p}, and by Lemma A.6(a) and Equation 4, deg⁡(u)<σ2<a​b≤k2\deg(u)<\sigma^{2}<ab\leq k^{2} for every u∈Uu\in U, so

|F|=∑u∈Udeg⁡(u)<k2​(4​k)p.|F|=\sum_{u\in U}\deg(u)<k^{2}(4k)^{p}\thinspace.

The time spent in this step sorting the vectors, running 𝖯𝖾𝖾𝗅\mathsf{Peel} and performing any sweep is O⁡(|F|​log2​|F|)=Op​(|F|​log2⁡(2​k))O(|F|\log_{2}|F|)=O_{p}(|F|\log_{2}(2k)), and the algorithm makes at least |F||F| queries to build HH. When a star is returned, the work in that step is linear in the number of queries. Summing over all steps and guesses, we obtain a time bound of Op​(log2⁡(2​k))O_{p}(\log_{2}(2k)) per query and hence Equation 16. ∎

Lemma B.3 (Distance from the starting vertex).

For sets X⊆LX\subseteq L and Y⊆RY\subseteq R returned by 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗇𝗌𝖾p​(G,v,k)\mathsf{LocalDense}_{p}(G,v,k), every vertex of X∪˙YX\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}Y lies within distance 1+p​log2⁡(4​k)/log2⁡(4/3)1+p\log_{2}(4k)/\log_{2}(4/3) of vv in GG. If v∈Lv\in L then d⁡(X∪{v},Y)≥d⁡(X,Y)/2d(X\cup\{v\},Y)\geq d(X,Y)/\sqrt{2}, and if v∈Rv\in R then d⁡(X,Y∪{v})≥d⁡(X,Y)/2d(X,Y\cup\{v\})\geq d(X,Y)/\sqrt{2}.

Proof of Lemma B.3.

In every search, supp⁡(x0)={v}\operatorname{supp}(x_{0})=\{v\}, and every vertex of supp⁡(xt+1)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t+1}) has a neighbor in supp⁡(xt)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}), since yt+1y_{t+1} is indexed by NG​(supp⁡(xt))N_{G}(\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})) and xt+1≤yt+1x_{t+1}\leq y_{t+1}. By induction, supp⁡(xt)\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}) lies within distance tt of vv. At step tt, the vertices of a returned star, of the sets returned by peeling and of the prefixes returned by the sweep lie in supp⁡(xt)∪˙NG​(supp⁡(xt))\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}N_{G}(\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})) and hence within distance t+1t+1 of vv. The initial edge is within distance one of vv. Every vector xtx_{t} is nonzero, so 1≤|supp⁡(xt)|≤(4​k)p​(3/4)t1\leq|\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})|\leq(4k)^{p}(3/4)^{t} by Lemma B.1(b), and thus t≤p​log2⁡(4​k)/log2⁡(4/3)t\leq p\log_{2}(4k)/\log_{2}(4/3).

For the last claim, if v∈Lv\in L, then e⁡(X∪{v},Y)≥e⁡(X,Y)e(X\cup\{v\},Y)\geq e(X,Y) and |X∪{v}|≤2​|X||X\cup\{v\}|\leq 2|X|, so d⁡(X∪{v},Y)≥d⁡(X,Y)/2d(X\cup\{v\},Y)\geq d(X,Y)/\sqrt{2}. The case v∈Rv\in R is symmetric. ∎

Appendix C The logarithmic factor at p=2p=2 and comparison with Andersen

Andersen’s guarantee has two parts: growth of the Euclidean norm inside a dense bipartite subgraph, and extraction of a dense bipartite subgraph from that growth (Section C.1). After recalling his iteration and the two lemmas, we describe the neighbor-query implementation of his algorithm in Section C.2. With the weak-ℓ2\ell_{2} bound Ix​(i)≤iI_{x}(i)\leq\sqrt{i} in place of the bound on ‖x‖p,∞\|x\|_{p,\infty}, we incur a logarithmic factor in the prefix-sum argument of Section 2.1 (Section C.3), and there is a weighted matrix for which the logarithmic factor in the extraction is necessary (Section C.4).

C.1 Andersen’s growth and extraction lemmas

Andersen’s iteration.

Andersen’s algorithm runs the pruned growth process [Andersen, 2010, Definition 5] for t0≔⌈log2⁡(2​k)⌉t_{0}\coloneq\lceil\log_{2}(2\sqrt{k})\rceil steps. Starting from x0≔1vx_{0}\coloneq\mathbbm{1}_{v}, with the pruning thresholds δt+1>0\delta_{t+1}>0 of that definition and the adjacency matrix AA of GG, it computes

yt+1≔xt​A‖xt​A‖2,xt+1≔prune⁡(δt+1,yt+1).y_{t+1}\coloneq\frac{x_{t}A}{\|x_{t}A\|_{2}},\qquad x_{t+1}\coloneq\operatorname{prune}(\delta_{t+1},y_{t+1})\thinspace.

Each yt+1y_{t+1} is a unit vector, so ‖xt‖2≤1\|x_{t}\|_{2}\leq 1.

Definition C.1 (Dyadic level sets [Andersen, 2010, Definition 6]).

For a nonnegative vector xx, its dyadic level sets are Dj​(x)≔{u:2−j−1<x⁡(u)≤2−j}D_{j}(x)\coloneq\{u:2^{-j-1}<x(u)\leq 2^{-j}\} for j∈Zj\in\mathbb Z.

At each step 0≤t<t00\leq t<t_{0}, Andersen’s algorithm tests the nonempty sets

X≔Di​(xt‖xt‖2),Y≔Dj​(xt​A‖xt​A‖2)with ​|i−j|≤4+log2⁡Δ.X\coloneq D_{i}\!\left(\frac{x_{t}}{\|x_{t}\|_{2}}\right),\qquad Y\coloneq D_{j}\!\left(\frac{x_{t}A}{\|x_{t}A\|_{2}}\right)\quad\text{with }|i-j|\leq 4+\log_{2}\Delta\thinspace.

It returns the tested sets X,YX,Y of maximum density.

Lemma C.2 (Growth inside a dense bipartite subgraph [Andersen, 2010, Lemma 2 and proof of Theorem 1]).

For S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R with e⁡(S,T)>0e(S,T)>0 and kk with |S|,|T|≤k|S|,|T|\leq k, there are S′⊆SS^{\prime}\subseteq S and T′⊆TT^{\prime}\subseteq T with e⁡(S′,T′)≥e⁡(S,T)/2e(S^{\prime},T^{\prime})\geq e(S,T)/2 such that every vertex of S′S^{\prime} has more than e⁡(S,T)/(4​|S|)e(S,T)/(4|S|) neighbors in T′T^{\prime} and every vertex of T′T^{\prime} has more than e⁡(S,T)/(4​|T|)e(S,T)/(4|T|) neighbors in S′S^{\prime}.

From every starting vertex v∈S′∪˙T′v\in S^{\prime}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T^{\prime}, the vectors of Andersen’s algorithm with parameter kk satisfy ‖xt​A‖2≥(d⁡(S,T)/16)​‖xt‖2\|x_{t}A\|_{2}\geq(d(S,T)/16)\|x_{t}\|_{2} for some t<t0t<t_{0}. If d⁡(S,T)<16d(S,T)<16, then also ‖x0​A‖2≥‖x0‖2\|x_{0}A\|_{2}\geq\|x_{0}\|_{2}.

For d⁡(S,T)≥16d(S,T)\geq 16, we apply Andersen’s proof of Theorem 1 with λ=d⁡(S,T)/16\lambda=d(S,T)/16. For the last claim, every v∈S′∪˙T′v\in S^{\prime}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T^{\prime} has a neighbor, so ‖x0​A‖2≥1=‖x0‖2\|x_{0}A\|_{2}\geq 1=\|x_{0}\|_{2}.

Lemma C.3 (From growth to dense level sets [Andersen, 2010, Lemma 1, weakened form]).

For a nonzero vector x≥0x\geq 0 supported on one side and λ≥1\lambda\geq 1 with ‖x​A‖2≥λ​‖x‖2\|xA\|_{2}\geq\lambda\|x\|_{2}, there are nonempty dyadic level sets XX of x/‖x‖2x/\|x\|_{2} and YY of x​A/‖x​A‖2xA/\|xA\|_{2} with d⁡(X,Y)d(X,Y) at least

λ72​(1+log2⁡(Δ/λ)).\frac{\lambda}{72\,(1+\log_{2}(\Delta/\lambda))}\thinspace. (18)

In Andersen’s Lemma 1, the density is at least λ/(72+16​log2⁡(Δ/λ))\lambda/(72+16\log_{2}(\Delta/\lambda)) for some level-set indices i,ji,j satisfying |i−j|≤4+log2⁡Δ|i-j|\leq 4+\log_{2}\Delta. Since λ≤Δ\lambda\leq\Delta, Equation 18 is weaker, and we state it without the restriction on the level-set indices.

C.2 Neighbor-query implementation of Andersen’s algorithm

As in Andersen’s proof of Theorem 2 [Andersen, 2010], the iteration in Section C.1 has |supp⁡(xt)|=O⁡(k2​4−t)|\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})|=O(k^{2}4^{-t}). At step tt, we read the adjacency list of each vertex u∈supp⁡(xt)u\in\operatorname{supp}(x_{t}) to its end, using deg⁡(u)+1≤Δ+1\deg(u)+1\leq\Delta+1 neighbor queries. Using the cached lists, we compute xt​Ax_{t}A and e⁡(X,Y)e(X,Y) for all level sets XX of xt/‖xt‖2x_{t}/\|x_{t}\|_{2} and YY of xt​A/‖xt​A‖2x_{t}A/\|x_{t}A\|_{2} without further queries. The total number of neighbor queries is therefore at most

(Δ+1)​∑t=0t0−1|supp⁡(xt)|=O⁡(Δ​k2),(\Delta+1)\sum_{t=0}^{t_{0}-1}|\operatorname{supp}(x_{t})|=O(\Delta k^{2})\thinspace,

since Δ≥1\Delta\geq 1 for a target of positive density. If Δ\Delta is unknown, we omit the restriction |i−j|≤4+log2⁡Δ|i-j|\leq 4+\log_{2}\Delta and consider all level sets X,YX,Y with e⁡(X,Y)>0e(X,Y)>0. No additional queries are needed, and the returned density is no smaller.

To bound the prefix sums of y​AyA by Cauchy–Schwarz, we need an upper bound on ‖y‖2\|y\|_{2}. We have bounded only ‖y‖2,∞\|y\|_{2,\infty}. For p>2p>2, by contrast, we can bound ‖y‖p,∞\|y\|_{p,\infty} in terms of ‖x‖p,∞\|x\|_{p,\infty} (Proposition A.4).

The logarithm in Andersen’s Lemma 1 also comes from a sum over logarithmically many scales: in its proof, he sums over all level-set indices i,ji,j with |i−j|≤4+log2⁡(Δ/λ)|i-j|\leq 4+\log_{2}(\Delta/\lambda).

The sum over all ranges is therefore Op​(1)O_{p}(1) times the largest of these bounds, and there is no logarithmic factor in Proposition A.4.

C.4 A tight example for norm-growth extraction

For nonnegative matrices, the logarithmic factor in Equation 18 is necessary [Bilu and Linial, 2006, see]. For a nonnegative matrix BB and nonempty sets S,TS,T of row and column indices, we write

dB​(S,T)≔∑u∈S∑w∈TBu​w|S|​|T|.d_{B}(S,T)\coloneq\frac{\sum_{u\in S}\sum_{w\in T}B_{uw}}{\sqrt{|S||T|}}\thinspace.

In Construction C.4, we define a symmetric matrix A¯\bar{A} and a vector ξL\xi_{L} with ‖ξL​A¯‖2=λ​‖ξL‖2\|\xi_{L}\bar{A}\|_{2}=\lambda\|\xi_{L}\|_{2} such that dA¯​(S,T)=O⁡(λ/log2⁡Δ)d_{\bar{A}}(S,T)=O(\lambda/\log_{2}\Delta) for all nonempty S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R, where Δ\Delta is the largest row sum.

Construction C.4.

For an integer ν≥1\nu\geq 1 and ζ≔2ν\zeta\coloneq 2^{\nu}, the sets LL and RR are partitioned into blocks Li,RiL_{i},R_{i} of size 4i4^{i} for i=0,…,ν−1i=0,\ldots,\nu-1. The symmetric matrix A¯\bar{A}, indexed by L∪˙RL\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}R, has entry ζ​2−i−j\zeta 2^{-i-j} between LiL_{i} and RjR_{j} and zero entries on L×LL\times L and R×RR\times R. The vector ξL\xi_{L} equals 2−i2^{-i} on LiL_{i} and zero on RR, the vector ξR\xi_{R} is defined symmetrically, and λ≔‖ξL​A¯‖2/‖ξL‖2\lambda\coloneq\|\xi_{L}\bar{A}\|_{2}/\|\xi_{L}\|_{2}.

Proposition C.5.

The matrix of Construction C.4 has spectral radius ν​ζ\nu\zeta and largest row sum Δ=ζ⁡(ζ−1)\Delta=\zeta(\zeta-1). Moreover,

λ=ν​ζ,ζ≤max∅≠S⊆L∅≠T⊆R⁡dA¯​(S,T)≤9​ζ.\lambda=\nu\zeta,\qquad\zeta\leq\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\varnothing\neq S\subseteq L\\ \varnothing\neq T\subseteq R\end{subarray}}d_{\bar{A}}(S,T)\leq 9\zeta\thinspace.

The nonempty dyadic level sets of ξL/‖ξL‖2\xi_{L}/\|\xi_{L}\|_{2} and ξL​A¯/‖ξL​A¯‖2\xi_{L}\bar{A}/\|\xi_{L}\bar{A}\|_{2} are L0,…,Lν−1L_{0},\ldots,L_{\nu-1} and R0,…,Rν−1R_{0},\ldots,R_{\nu-1}, respectively. Every block density dA¯​(Li,Rj)d_{\bar{A}}(L_{i},R_{j}) equals ζ\zeta. The ratio of λ\lambda to the maximum of dA¯​(S,T)d_{\bar{A}}(S,T) over nonempty S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R is Θ⁡(ν)=Θ⁡(log2⁡Δ)\Theta(\nu)=\Theta(\log_{2}\Delta). The right-hand side of Equation 18, evaluated at λ=ν​ζ\lambda=\nu\zeta, is Θ⁡(ζ)\Theta(\zeta).

Proof.

For u∈Rju\in R_{j} with 0≤j<ν0\leq j<\nu, the contribution from each left block LiL_{i} to (ξL​A¯)​(u)(\xi_{L}\bar{A})(u) is 4i⋅2−i⋅ζ​2−i−j=ζ​2−j4^{i}\cdot 2^{-i}\cdot\zeta 2^{-i-j}=\zeta 2^{-j}, so

(ξL​A¯)​(u)=ν​ζ​2−j=ν​ζ​ξR​(u).(\xi_{L}\bar{A})(u)=\nu\zeta 2^{-j}=\nu\zeta\,\xi_{R}(u)\thinspace.

By symmetry, ξR​A¯=ν​ζ​ξL\xi_{R}\bar{A}=\nu\zeta\,\xi_{L}, so ξL+ξR\xi_{L}+\xi_{R} is a positive eigenvector with eigenvalue ν​ζ\nu\zeta, which is therefore the spectral radius. Since ‖ξL‖2=‖ξR‖2=ν\|\xi_{L}\|_{2}=\|\xi_{R}\|_{2}=\sqrt{\nu}, λ=ν​ζ\lambda=\nu\zeta. By direct summation, the largest row sum is Δ=ζ⁡(ζ−1)\Delta=\zeta(\zeta-1), and dA¯​(Li,Rj)=ζd_{\bar{A}}(L_{i},R_{j})=\zeta for all i,ji,j. Consecutive block values differ by a factor of two, so the nonempty dyadic level sets are exactly the blocks.

For nonempty S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R, we write si≔|S∩Li|s_{i}\coloneq|S\cap L_{i}| and take the integer q≥0q\geq 0 with |S|≤2q<2​|S|\sqrt{|S|}\leq 2^{q}<2\sqrt{|S|}. Since si≤4is_{i}\leq 4^{i},

∑i=0ν−1si​2−i≤∑i=0q−12i+2−q​|S|≤2q+|S|​2−q≤3​|S|.\sum_{i=0}^{\nu-1}s_{i}2^{-i}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}2^{i}+2^{-q}|S|\leq 2^{q}+|S|2^{-q}\leq 3\sqrt{|S|}\thinspace.

We apply the same bound to tj≔|T∩Rj|t_{j}\coloneq|T\cap R_{j}| and obtain

∑u∈S∑w∈TA¯u​w=ζ⁡(∑i=0ν−1si​2−i)​(∑j=0ν−1tj​2−j)≤9​ζ​|S|​|T|.\sum_{u\in S}\sum_{w\in T}\bar{A}_{uw}=\zeta\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{\nu-1}s_{i}2^{-i}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{\nu-1}t_{j}2^{-j}\Bigr)\leq 9\zeta\sqrt{|S||T|}\thinspace.

Finally, since Δ=ζ⁡(ζ−1)\Delta=\zeta(\zeta-1) and λ=ν​ζ\lambda=\nu\zeta, both log2⁡Δ\log_{2}\Delta and 1+log2⁡(Δ/λ)1+\log_{2}(\Delta/\lambda) are Θ⁡(ν)\Theta(\nu), so the right-hand side of Equation 18 is Θ⁡(ζ)\Theta(\zeta). ∎

Appendix D Lower bounds

Since sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)=Ω⁡(k)d(X,Y)=\Omega(k) have Ω⁡(k2)\Omega(k^{2}) edges between them, an output of o⁡(k2)o(k^{2}) vertices per side must have many more edges than vertices, as the target does, and the algorithm has to find these edges. The query lower bound is proved by hiding a complete bipartite graph at uniformly chosen adjacency-list positions (Section D.1), and the computational lower bounds by reducing Densest kk-Subgraph to the local problem (Section D.2).

Definition D.1.

An algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} receives a starting vertex vv, an integer k≥1k\geq 1, and neighbor-query access to a simple bipartite graph GG, as specified in the graph-access model of Section B.2. The algorithm has output bound ϕ\phi if, for every input, it returns either ⊥\bot or nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L, Y⊆RY\subseteq R with |X|,|Y|≤ϕ⁡(k)|X|,|Y|\leq\phi(k). Unless we explicitly allow randomness, algorithms are deterministic; for randomized algorithms, all output, query, and running-time bounds hold for every choice of the internal randomness, and success probabilities are over that randomness. Unless we impose a running-time bound, computation between queries is unrestricted.

D.1 The query lower bound

Theorem D.2 (Queries sublinear in Δ\Delta).

For a constant 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1 and ϕ⁡(k)=o⁡(k2)\phi(k)=o(k^{2}), if a possibly randomized algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} as in Definition D.1 has output bound ϕ\phi and makes at most q⁡(k,Δ)q(k,\Delta) queries on every input, where q⁡(k,Δ)=o⁡(Δ)q(k,\Delta)=o(\Delta) as Δ→∞\Delta\to\infty for every fixed kk, then, for every sufficiently large kk, there is a simple bipartite graph GG containing a complete bipartite subgraph with sides S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R of kk vertices each, such that from every v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T the output of 𝖠\mathsf{A} is ⊥\bot or has density below ρ​k\rho k with probability at least 2/32/3.

Proof of Theorem D.2.

For the extension to randomized algorithms, we use a transcript-coupling approach inspired by Peng et al. [2026, Section 5.2]. Since ϕ⁡(k)=o⁡(k2)\phi(k)=o(k^{2}), we can fix any sufficiently large kk with 2​ϕ​(k)<ρ​k\sqrt{2\phi(k)}<\rho k. Choose integers N>kN>k and then Δ≥k\Delta\geq k so that

2​k2​q​(k,Δ)Δ+4​ϕ​(k)​k2N−1<13,\frac{2k^{2}q(k,\Delta)}{\Delta}+\frac{4\phi(k)k^{2}}{N-1}<\frac{1}{3},

which is possible because q⁡(k,Δ)=o⁡(Δ)q(k,\Delta)=o(\Delta) for fixed kk. Let G0G_{0} consist of NN disjoint stars centered on each side, each with Δ\Delta leaves, with fixed vertex identifiers and adjacency-list orders. Choose SS and TT independently and uniformly among the kk-subsets of the left and right centers, respectively. For each chosen center, independently select kk of the Δ\Delta positions in its adjacency list uniformly, and replace the entries at those positions by the kk target centers on the opposite side in identifier order. Isolate the corresponding leaves, keeping all vertex identifiers. The resulting graph GG is simple and bipartite, every center still has degree Δ\Delta, and S,TS,T span a complete bipartite subgraph of density kk.

Fix a center vv and condition on v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T. Fix the internal randomness of 𝖠\mathsf{A} independently of the construction, and compare its runs from vv on G0G_{0} and GG using this same randomness. The run on G0G_{0} is independent of the chosen target and positions. Each query in that run concerns at most one original star edge, either through its position in a center’s list or through a query at its leaf. Conditional on v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T, each such edge is replaced with probability at most k/Δk/\Delta. Until a differing answer is received, the two computations coincide. By a union bound over the at most q⁡(k,Δ)q(k,\Delta) queries on G0G_{0}, the probability of any differing answer is at most k​q​(k,Δ)/Δkq(k,\Delta)/\Delta.

The output on G0G_{0} contains at most 2​ϕ​(k)2\phi(k) centers. Each center other than vv belongs to S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T with conditional probability at most k/(N−1)k/(N-1), so the probability that the output contains another target center is at most 2​ϕ​(k)​k/(N−1)2\phi(k)k/(N-1). If neither event occurs, the output on GG is the same as on G0G_{0} and contains no edge of S×TS\times T. If it is a pair (X,Y)(X,Y) rather than ⊥\bot, all its edges belong to G0G_{0}. Writing e0≔eG0​(X,Y)e_{0}\coloneq e_{G_{0}}(X,Y), we have e0≤|X|+|Y|≤2​ϕ​(k)e_{0}\leq|X|+|Y|\leq 2\phi(k) since G0G_{0} is a forest, and e0≤|X|​|Y|e_{0}\leq|X||Y|. Thus

dG​(X,Y)≤e0|X|​|Y|≤e0≤2​ϕ​(k)<ρ​k.d_{G}(X,Y)\leq\frac{e_{0}}{\sqrt{|X||Y|}}\leq\sqrt{e_{0}}\leq\sqrt{2\phi(k)}<\rho k.

Let pv​(G)p_{v}(G) be the probability, over the internal randomness of 𝖠\mathsf{A}, of returning sets of density at least ρ​k\rho k from vv on GG. Averaging also over that randomness in the preceding bounds, we obtain

E⁡[pv​(G)∣v∈S∪˙T]≤k​q​(k,Δ)Δ+2​ϕ​(k)​kN−1,\mathbb E\!\left[p_{v}(G)\mid v\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T\right]\leq\frac{kq(k,\Delta)}{\Delta}+\frac{2\phi(k)k}{N-1},

where the expectation is over the random construction. There are 2​N2N centers, each belonging to S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T with probability k/Nk/N, so

E⁡[∑v∈S∪˙Tpv​(G)]≤2​k2​q​(k,Δ)Δ+4​ϕ​(k)​k2N−1<13.\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{v\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T}p_{v}(G)\right]\leq\frac{2k^{2}q(k,\Delta)}{\Delta}+\frac{4\phi(k)k^{2}}{N-1}<\frac{1}{3}.

Corollary D.3 (Approximation and output size with restricted queries).

For α⁡(k)≥1\alpha(k)\geq 1 with α⁡(k)=o⁡(k)\alpha(k)=o(k) and ϕ⁡(k)=o⁡(k2/α​(k)2)\phi(k)=o(k^{2}/\alpha(k)^{2}), if a possibly randomized algorithm as in Definition D.1 has output bound ϕ\phi and makes at most q⁡(k,Δ)q(k,\Delta) queries, where q⁡(k,Δ)=o⁡(Δ)q(k,\Delta)=o(\Delta) as Δ→∞\Delta\to\infty for every fixed kk, then, for every sufficiently large kk, there is a simple bipartite graph containing a complete bipartite subgraph with sides S,TS,T of kk vertices each, such that, from every v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T, the algorithm returns ⊥\bot or sets of density below d⁡(S,T)/α⁡(k)d(S,T)/\alpha(k) with probability at least 2/32/3.

Proof.

We apply the construction in the proof of Theorem D.2 with ρ=1/α⁡(k)\rho=1/\alpha(k), since its condition 2​ϕ​(k)<ρ​k\sqrt{2\phi(k)}<\rho k holds for all sufficiently large kk:

α⁡(k)k​2​ϕ​(k)=2​α​(k)2​ϕ​(k)k2<1,\frac{\alpha(k)}{k}\sqrt{2\phi(k)}=\sqrt{\frac{2\alpha(k)^{2}\phi(k)}{k^{2}}}<1\thinspace,

as the expression tends to zero. For each such kk, choose NN and Δ\Delta as in that proof. From every target vertex of the resulting fixed graph, the algorithm returns ⊥\bot or sets of density below k/α⁡(k)=d⁡(S,T)/α⁡(k)k/\alpha(k)=d(S,T)/\alpha(k) with probability at least 2/32/3. ∎

D.2 Computational lower bounds

For both lower bounds under SPCH and ETH, we use the same reduction. In Section D.2.1, we construct a dense subgraph on kk vertices of a graph JJ from the outputs of a local algorithm on its bipartite double cover, and in Sections D.2.2 and D.2.3, we prove the two lower bounds. Polynomial time means time polynomial in the number of vertices of the input graph, uniformly over all kk up to that number.

D.2.1 Reduction from Densest kk-Subgraph

For a simple graph JJ on NN vertices, eJ​(U)e_{J}(U) is the number of edges induced by U⊆V⁡(J)U\subseteq V(J), and the bipartite double cover GG of JJ has two copies L,RL,R of V⁡(J)V(J) and edges uL​wR,wL​uRu_{L}w_{R},w_{L}u_{R} for every u​w∈E⁡(J)uw\in E(J). The graph GG has 2​N2N vertices, and each vertex of GG has the same degree as the corresponding vertex of JJ, which is below NN. For k≥2k\geq 2, the two copies S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R of a kk-clique in JJ are cohesive with d⁡(S,T)=k−1d(S,T)=k-1, since every vertex has k−1k-1 neighbors in the opposite set.

Lemma D.4 (Extracting a dense kk-vertex subgraph).

For a simple graph JJ on at least k≥2k\geq 2 vertices and its bipartite double cover GG, 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1, B≥1B\geq 1, and nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L and Y⊆RY\subseteq R with |X|,|Y|≤B​k|X|,|Y|\leq Bk and d⁡(X,Y)≥ρ⁡(k−1)d(X,Y)\geq\rho(k-1), a set UU of kk vertices of JJ can be found in polynomial time with

eJ​(U)≥ρ216​B​(k2).e_{J}(U)\geq\frac{\rho^{2}}{16B}\binom{k}{2}\thinspace.
Proof.

For h≔⌊k/2⌋h\coloneq\lfloor k/2\rfloor, we take X′X^{\prime} to be the min⁡{|X|,h}\min\{|X|,h\} vertices of XX with the most neighbors in YY, and Y′Y^{\prime} the min⁡{|Y|,h}\min\{|Y|,h\} vertices of YY with the most neighbors in X′X^{\prime}.

Since |X′|+|Y′|≤2​h≤k|X^{\prime}|+|Y^{\prime}|\leq 2h\leq k, we form UU from the corresponding vertices of JJ, adding arbitrary vertices until |U|=k|U|=k. Each edge of JJ has at most two copies in the double cover, so eJ​(U)≥e⁡(X′,Y′)/2e_{J}(U)\geq e(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})/2.

The vertices of X′X^{\prime} have average degree into YY at least e⁡(X,Y)/|X|e(X,Y)/|X|, so e⁡(X′,Y)≥(|X′|/|X|)​e​(X,Y)e(X^{\prime},Y)\geq(|X^{\prime}|/|X|)e(X,Y), and similarly e⁡(X′,Y′)≥(|Y′|/|Y|)​e​(X′,Y)e(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})\geq(|Y^{\prime}|/|Y|)e(X^{\prime},Y). Therefore,

e⁡(X′,Y′)≥|X′||X|​|Y′||Y|​e​(X,Y)=h2​e​(X,Y)max⁡{|X|,h}​max​{|Y|,h}.e(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})\geq\frac{|X^{\prime}|}{|X|}\frac{|Y^{\prime}|}{|Y|}e(X,Y)=\frac{h^{2}e(X,Y)}{\max\{|X|,h\}\max\{|Y|,h\}}\thinspace.

By the density assumption, e⁡(X,Y)≥ρ⁡(k−1)​|X|​|Y|e(X,Y)\geq\rho(k-1)\sqrt{|X||Y|} and, since d⁡(X,Y)≤e⁡(X,Y)d(X,Y)\leq\sqrt{e(X,Y)}, also e⁡(X,Y)≥ρ2​(k−1)2e(X,Y)\geq\rho^{2}(k-1)^{2}. If one side has at most hh vertices, one factor in the denominator of the averaging bound is hh and the other is at most B​kBk. We therefore keep at least an h/(B​k)h/(Bk) fraction of the edges, so e⁡(X′,Y′)≥h​ρ2​(k−1)2/(B​k)e(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})\geq h\rho^{2}(k-1)^{2}/(Bk). Otherwise, |X|,|Y|>h|X|,|Y|>h, so the denominator in the averaging bound is |X|​|Y||X||Y|. Since |X|​|Y|≤B​k\sqrt{|X||Y|}\leq Bk,

e⁡(X′,Y′)≥h2​ρ​(k−1)|X|​|Y|≥h2​ρ​(k−1)B​k≥h​ρ2​(k−1)22​B​k,e(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})\geq\frac{h^{2}\rho(k-1)}{\sqrt{|X||Y|}}\geq\frac{h^{2}\rho(k-1)}{Bk}\geq\frac{h\rho^{2}(k-1)^{2}}{2Bk}\thinspace,

using h≥(k−1)/2h\geq(k-1)/2 and ρ≤1\rho\leq 1. In either case,

eJ​(U)≥h​ρ2​(k−1)24​B​k≥ρ216​B​(k2),e_{J}(U)\geq\frac{h\rho^{2}(k-1)^{2}}{4Bk}\geq\frac{\rho^{2}}{16B}\binom{k}{2}\thinspace,

using h≥(k−1)/2h\geq(k-1)/2 and k−1≥k/2k-1\geq k/2. ∎

Lemma D.5.

For a simple graph JJ on N≥k≥2N\geq k\geq 2 vertices and its bipartite double cover GG, 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1, B≥1B\geq 1, and an algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} that returns ⊥\bot or nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L and Y⊆RY\subseteq R with |X|,|Y|≤B​k|X|,|Y|\leq Bk from every v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), we can find, with 2​N2N calls to 𝖠\mathsf{A} and polynomial additional time, a set UU of kk vertices of JJ such that, if 𝖠⁡(G,v,k)\mathsf{A}(G,v,k) returns sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)≥ρ⁡(k−1)d(X,Y)\geq\rho(k-1) for some vv, then

eJ​(U)≥ρ216​B​(k2).e_{J}(U)\geq\frac{\rho^{2}}{16B}\binom{k}{2}\thinspace.
Proof.

We run 𝖠\mathsf{A} from every vertex of GG, apply the construction in Lemma D.4 to each output X,YX,Y, and keep a set inducing the most edges. If every call returns ⊥\bot, we take any kk vertices. If 𝖠\mathsf{A} returns sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)≥ρ⁡(k−1)d(X,Y)\geq\rho(k-1), then by Lemma D.4 the corresponding set of kk vertices satisfies the claimed bound, as does the set we keep. We construct the double cover and select the sets of kk vertices in polynomial time. ∎

D.2.2 The limitation under SPCH

Definition D.6 (Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis [Manurangsi et al., 2021, Hypothesis 1]).

The Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis (SPCH) is the assumption that, for some 0<θ<1/20<\theta<1/2, no randomized algorithm running in time no⁡(log2⁡n)n^{o(\log_{2}n)} distinguishes the random graph 𝒢⁡(n,12)\mathcal{G}(n,\frac{1}{2}) on nn vertices, in which each edge is present independently with probability 1/21/2, from the same graph 𝒢⁡(n,12,⌈nθ⌉)\mathcal{G}(n,\frac{1}{2},\lceil n^{\theta}\rceil) with a clique added on ⌈nθ⌉\lceil n^{\theta}\rceil uniformly chosen vertices, with success probability at least 2/32/3 under each distribution. We call these the no and yes distributions, respectively. The probability is over the input graph and the algorithm’s randomness.

We use the following hardness theorem for Densest kk-Subgraph, with the promise that the input contains a kk-clique.

Theorem D.7 ([Manurangsi et al., 2021, Theorem 2]).

Assuming SPCH, for every β\beta with β⁡(k)=o⁡(k)\beta(k)=o(k) and every computable ff, no algorithm, given an NN-vertex graph JJ and kk such that JJ contains a kk-clique, returns in time f⁡(k)​NO⁡(1)f(k)N^{O(1)} a set UU of kk vertices with

eJ​(U)≥1β⁡(k)​(k2).e_{J}(U)\geq\frac{1}{\beta(k)}\binom{k}{2}\thinspace.
Theorem D.8 (Limitations on the output size under SPCH).

Assuming SPCH, for a constant 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1 and ϕ⁡(k)=o⁡(k2)\phi(k)=o(k^{2}), if a possibly randomized algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} as in Definition D.1 has output bound ϕ\phi and runs in time f⁡(k)​|V|O⁡(1)f(k)|V|^{O(1)} on every input (G,v,k)(G,v,k), for a computable function ff of kk alone, then, for some k≥2k\geq 2, there is a simple bipartite graph GG with cohesive sets S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R of kk vertices each, such that from every v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T the output is ⊥\bot or has density below ρ​d​(S,T)\rho\,d(S,T) with probability greater than 1/31/3.

Proof of Theorem D.8.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that for every k≥2k\geq 2 and all cohesive target sets S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R of kk vertices each, the algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} returns sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)≥ρ​d​(S,T)d(X,Y)\geq\rho\,d(S,T) from some v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T with probability at least 2/32/3. For JJ with a kk-clique, the two copies S,TS,T of the clique in the double cover are cohesive with d⁡(S,T)=k−1d(S,T)=k-1. We run 𝖠\mathsf{A} from every vertex of GG and form a set of kk vertices of JJ from each returned pair X,YX,Y as in the proof of Lemma D.4. Among these sets, we keep one with the most edges between its vertices. By Lemma D.5 with B=1+ϕ⁡(k)/kB=1+\phi(k)/k, we can find a set UU of kk vertices inducing at least (k2)/β⁡(k)\binom{k}{2}/\beta(k) edges with probability at least 2/32/3, where

β⁡(k)≔16​(k+ϕ​(k))ρ2​k=o⁡(k).\beta(k)\coloneq\frac{16(k+\phi(k))}{\rho^{2}k}=o(k)\thinspace.

We can compute eJ​(U)e_{J}(U) for each returned set, so we repeat the procedure in Lemma D.5 independently a constant number of times (concretely, five) and keep a set inducing the most edges. The subgraph induced by this set contains at least (k2)/β⁡(k)\binom{k}{2}/\beta(k) edges with probability at least 1−3−5>0.991-3^{-5}>0.99. The running time is f′​(k)​NO⁡(1)f^{\prime}(k)N^{O(1)} for a computable f′f^{\prime}.

In the reduction from planted clique in Manurangsi et al. [2021, Section 4.1], completeness and soundness each hold with probability at least 0.90.9. We use the procedure in Lemma D.5, with the five independent repetitions, as the Densest kk-Subgraph algorithm in that reduction. We then distinguish the yes and no distributions of SPCH (Definition D.6) with success probability at least 0.9⋅0.99>2/30.9\cdot 0.99>2/3 under each distribution, contradicting SPCH. ∎

Remark.

We do not require β\beta in Theorem D.7 to be nondecreasing. In Manurangsi et al. [2021, Section 4.1], the ratio is a function g⁡(k)≤kg(k)\leq k growing with kk, so we replace β\beta with the nondecreasing β~​(k)≔max1≤j≤k⁡β⁡(j)\tilde{\beta}(k)\coloneq\max_{1\leq j\leq k}\beta(j). For every δ>0\delta>0, with Cδ≥0C_{\delta}\geq 0 bounding β⁡(j)\beta(j) for the finitely many jj with β⁡(j)>δ​j\beta(j)>\delta j, β~​(k)≤max⁡{Cδ,δ​k}\tilde{\beta}(k)\leq\max\{C_{\delta},\delta k\}, so β~=o⁡(k)\tilde{\beta}=o(k). In particular, β~​(k)≤k\tilde{\beta}(k)\leq k for all sufficiently large kk, and exhaustive search handles the remaining values of kk.

Corollary D.9 (Approximation and output size under SPCH).

Assuming SPCH, for α⁡(k)≥1\alpha(k)\geq 1 with α⁡(k)=o⁡(k)\alpha(k)=o(\sqrt{k}) and ϕ⁡(k)=o⁡(k2/α​(k)2)\phi(k)=o(k^{2}/\alpha(k)^{2}), no algorithm as in Definition D.1 with output bound ϕ\phi and running time f⁡(k)​|V|O⁡(1)f(k)|V|^{O(1)} for a computable ff guarantees, for every k≥2k\geq 2 and every cohesive target S,TS,T of kk vertices per side, an output of density at least d⁡(S,T)/α⁡(k)d(S,T)/\alpha(k) from some starting vertex in S∪˙TS\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T.

Proof.

For such an algorithm, by Lemma D.5 with ρ=1/α⁡(k)\rho=1/\alpha(k) and B=1+ϕ⁡(k)/kB=1+\phi(k)/k, we obtain an approximation ratio β⁡(k)≔16​α​(k)2​(k+ϕ⁡(k))/k\beta(k)\coloneq 16\alpha(k)^{2}(k+\phi(k))/k for Densest kk-Subgraph, with

β⁡(k)k=16​(α​(k)2k+α​(k)2​ϕ​(k)k2)⟶0.\frac{\beta(k)}{k}=16\left(\frac{\alpha(k)^{2}}{k}+\frac{\alpha(k)^{2}\phi(k)}{k^{2}}\right)\longrightarrow 0\thinspace.

The running time is f′​(k)​NO⁡(1)f^{\prime}(k)N^{O(1)} for a computable f′f^{\prime}, contradicting Theorem D.7. Following the proof of Theorem D.8 with ρ=1/α⁡(k)\rho=1/\alpha(k), we also rule out algorithms that use randomness, always respect the bounds on output size and running time, and succeed with probability at least 2/32/3. ∎

Quadratic output on the reduction instances.

When JJ contains a kk-clique, we can achieve a quadratic output bound on its bipartite double cover in time kO⁡(k)​NO⁡(1)k^{O(k)}N^{O(1)}. If a vertex of JJ has at least k2k^{2} neighbors, one of its copies and k2k^{2} of that copy’s neighbors form a star of density kk. Otherwise, every neighborhood in JJ has fewer than k2k^{2} vertices, and we find the promised kk-clique by testing all (k−1)(k-1)-subsets of each neighborhood together with its center. The two copies of the clique have density k−1k-1. Thus, on these instances, subquadratic output is essential to the lower bound even with full graph access.

D.2.3 The limitation under ETH

Definition D.10 (Exponential Time Hypothesis [Impagliazzo and Paturi, 2001]).

The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is the assumption that 3-SAT for formulas with mm clauses cannot be decided in time 2o⁡(m)2^{o(m)}. By the sparsification lemma of Impagliazzo et al. [2001], this is equivalent to the formulation in terms of variables.

We use the following hardness theorem, in which the graph contains a kk-clique in the yes case.

Theorem D.11 ([Manurangsi, 2017, Theorem 1]).

Assuming ETH, there is a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that no polynomial-time algorithm, given a graph JJ on N≥4N\geq 4 vertices and an integer 2≤k≤N2\leq k\leq N, distinguishes the case that JJ contains a kk-clique from the case that every kk-vertex subgraph of JJ contains at most (k2)/χ⁡(N)\binom{k}{2}/\chi(N) edges, where

χ⁡(N)≔N1/(log2⁡log2​N)c0.\chi(N)\coloneq N^{1/(\log_{2}\log_{2}N)^{c_{0}}}\thinspace.
Theorem D.12 (Limitations on the output size under ETH).

Assuming ETH, for constants 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1 and c≥1c\geq 1, if a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} returns ⊥\bot or nonempty sets X⊆LX\subseteq L and Y⊆RY\subseteq R with |X|,|Y|≤c​k​log2c⁡(2+k+Δ)|X|,|Y|\leq c\,k\log_{2}^{c}(2+k+\Delta) on every input (G,v,k)(G,v,k), then, for some k≥2k\geq 2, there is a simple bipartite graph GG with cohesive sets S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R of kk vertices each, such that from every v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T the output is ⊥\bot or has density below ρ​d​(S,T)\rho\,d(S,T). The same conclusion holds for running time polynomial in kk, Δ\Delta and log2⁡|V|\log_{2}|V|.

Proof.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that for all cohesive target sets S⊆LS\subseteq L and T⊆RT\subseteq R, the algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} returns sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)≥ρ​d​(S,T)d(X,Y)\geq\rho\,d(S,T) from some v∈S∪˙Tv\in S\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}T. For an NN-vertex graph JJ and k≤Nk\leq N, the double cover has Δ<N\Delta<N, so the output bound is at most B​kBk for B≔c​⌈log2⁡(4​N)⌉cB\coloneq c\lceil\log_{2}(4N)\rceil^{c}, and we apply the procedure of Lemma D.5. If JJ contains a kk-clique, its two copies S,TS,T are cohesive with d⁡(S,T)=k−1d(S,T)=k-1, so 𝖠\mathsf{A} returns sets X,YX,Y with d⁡(X,Y)≥ρ⁡(k−1)d(X,Y)\geq\rho(k-1) from some vertex, and the set UU of Lemma D.5 satisfies

eJ​(U)≥ρ216​B​(k2)>1χ⁡(N)​(k2)e_{J}(U)\geq\frac{\rho^{2}}{16B}\binom{k}{2}>\frac{1}{\chi(N)}\binom{k}{2}\thinspace

for all sufficiently large NN, since χ⁡(N)\chi(N) grows faster than every power of log2⁡N\log_{2}N. In the other case of the promise, every set of kk vertices, including UU, induces at most (k2)/χ⁡(N)\binom{k}{2}/\chi(N) edges. By comparing eJ​(U)e_{J}(U) with (k2)/χ⁡(N)\binom{k}{2}/\chi(N), we can therefore distinguish the two cases of Theorem D.11 in polynomial time, with exhaustive search for bounded NN. Finally, a running time polynomial in kk, Δ\Delta and log2⁡|V|\log_{2}|V| is polynomial in |V||V| when k≤|V|k\leq|V| and Δ<|V|\Delta<|V|. ∎

Why the limitation under ETH is weaker.

We cannot obtain the quadratic bound of Theorem D.8 from the hard instances used under ETH, because they have N=k1+o⁡(1)N=k^{1+o(1)} vertices. Manurangsi [2017, Section 3.2] constructs graphs whose vertices are partial assignments to ℓ\ell of the nn variables of a 3-SAT formula. Each graph has N=2ℓ​(nℓ)N=2^{\ell}\binom{n}{\ell} vertices. If the formula is satisfiable, the restrictions of a satisfying assignment to all ℓ\ell-element sets of variables form a clique of size k=(nℓ)k=\binom{n}{\ell}. With the parameter choices in that proof, ℓ=o⁡(n)\ell=o(n). Hence

log2⁡Nlog2⁡k=1+ℓlog2⁡k≤1+1log2⁡(n/ℓ)=1+o⁡(1).\frac{\log_{2}N}{\log_{2}k}=1+\frac{\ell}{\log_{2}k}\leq 1+\frac{1}{\log_{2}(n/\ell)}=1+o(1)\thinspace.

For fixed 0<δ<10<\delta<1 and large kk, the entire double cover has fewer than k2−δk^{2-\delta} vertices per side, and nonempty subsets X⊆LX\subseteq L and Y⊆RY\subseteq R maximizing d⁡(X,Y)d(X,Y) can then be found in polynomial time [Charikar, 2000, Section 4, Theorem 3], meeting the output bound k2−δk^{2-\delta} with approximation ratio one.
